title: GM sold driving behaviour to firms that feed insurers
hook: Your hard braking and late-night drives could reach your insurance price.
collected: Precise location and driving behaviour (speeding, hard braking, late-night driving) from GM cars through OnStar 'Smart Driver'.
howObtained: Connected-car systems; the FTC said enrolment was often pushed during car purchase without clear disclosure.
done: The FTC alleged GM sold this data to consumer reporting agencies. New York Times reporting (March 2024) named LexisNexis and Verisk, and drivers said their insurance rose.
affected: Owners of millions of GM vehicles.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC final order. GM did not admit wrongdoing. The names of the recipients come from NYT reporting (REPORTED); GM confirmed sharing 'certain insights'.

companyResponse.text: GM said it stopped sharing with LexisNexis and Verisk in March 2024, and that the FTC had formally approved the agreement reached the year before.
companyResponse.source: GM statements via NYT and TechCrunch

outcome.text: Five-year ban on sharing location and driving data with consumer reporting agencies; consent, access and deletion rights for 20 years. No money. Texas also sued in August 2024 (ALLEGED).

sources.title: FTC Finalizes Order Settling Allegations GM and OnStar Collected and Sold Geolocation Data
The FTC's data-sharing order against GM is finally settled

limits: How much the scores changed individual premiums is not documented in the order. LexisNexis said the score was one factor of many.
whyItMatters: Your car can act like a credit bureau's informant.

title: Texas v. Allstate and Arity: driving data collected through other apps
hook: The state says a fuel-rewards or family-locator app may have been scoring your driving.
collected: Location (as often as every 15 seconds), accelerometer and gyroscope readings, and phone pick-ups while driving, according to Texas.
howObtained: Arity's software kit embedded in apps such as Life360, GasBuddy, Fuel Rewards and Routely, per the lawsuit.
done: Texas alleges the data was sold and used to set insurance prices, covering more than 45 million Americans.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: State lawsuit; the first under a comprehensive state privacy law. No ruling yet.

companyResponse.text: Allstate says Arity helps consumers get the most accurate auto insurance price after they consent in a simple and transparent way.

sources.title: Texas sues Allstate over data privacy
Attorney General Ken Paxton Sues Allstate and Arity

whyItMatters: SDKs can move data between apps that seem to have nothing to do with each other.
